subtopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS OF HOUSE

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS OF HOUSE
speechtext:
If hon. members will give me leave to make a brief statement about the use of routine proceedings, I think this might be an appropriate time to do so and to consider routine proceedings in so far as ministerial statements and oral questions without notice are part of those proceedings.
As hon. gentlemen appreciate, time is given at the beginning of each sitting of the house for routine proceedings, because they are routine or formal in their nature; matters which with few exceptions are dealt with without debate. They are proceedings which require attention, but not much time, before the house enters upon the orders of the day and the substantial business before it.
Although there are exceptional days when routine proceedings are not accomplished quickly, if the past is any criterion for the future routine proceedings should be concluded within approximately half an hour of the beginning of the sitting. Perhaps it is desirable that this should be so. If too many or too long ministerial statements are made and commented upon by two hon. members, as the situation is now, from opposition parties, and if hon. members do not limit their oral questions in accordance with the established practice, it will be at the expense of the time for the debate of matters appearing on the order paper.
Ministerial statements should relate to matters of importance and should be as brief as the subject matter permits; they should not be provocative in their nature. In saying these things I am not referring to any particular incident but to the practice of the house in general, about which, it seems to me, we should remind ourselves at the beginning of a session. The comments on ministerial statements should also be brief and unprovocative, or temperate at least, and should not become a debate in any sense of the word but a preliminary comment with such reservations as may be felt necessary with respect to future discussion of the subject.
May I say, too, that a ministerial statement should not be introduced in answer to a question unless the statement itself is of such brevity and urgency that it can be accepted as an answer to a question in accordance with the practice relating to oral questions.
130	HOUSE OF
Statement by Mr. Speaker
On the subject of oral questions, other Speakers have found it desirable from time to time to remind the house of the practice as it has been followed and as it has been explained in the commentaries on our procedure so that there might be harmony between the Speakers and the house in the application of those principles, and the avoidance of unnecessary argument. In the past, following that practice, Mr. Speaker Macdonald made a very precise and excellent statement on the practice with respect to oral statements which I commend to the attention of all members of the house. Perhaps they will make a note of it, because I do not propose to read at any length. This statement will be found in the Journals for 1951 at pages 427 and 428. Mr. Speaker Beaudoin made a comprehensive review of the practice on March 16, 1956 and this may be found at the beginning of page 2206 of Hansard for that year. I myself made a statement on October 17, 1957.
If I may be permitted a moment more I should like to read what appears to me to be the essential practice as it is explained in Hansard and in the citations in Beauchesne. The standing orders-that is standing orders 39, 40 and 41-provide only for written questions to be answered by the tabling of written answers or, if the question is marked with an asterisk, to be answered orally on Wednesday within the first hour or on other days after the last order of business. Other oral questions asked upon the calling of orders of the day are sanctioned only by usage. Beauchesne in the fourth edition, citation 173, paragraph 1 says:
The practice has been so long and so regularly in the house that, if not impossible, in my opinion, it would be inadvisable to stop it. It seems to me manifestly unfair to compel ministers to answer questions on important matters without an opportunity to consult their chief officers; and it would be arbitrary to deprive private members of putting certain questions of immediate urgency on the orders of the day being called.
The following principles have been applied to oral questions:
1.	The question should seek information or press for action on a matter relating to public affairs of such immediate urgency that it would be improper to put it on the order paper. I remind hon. members that the order paper is the normal way of getting information which can be given in answer to a question.
2.	Both questions and answers should be concise, factual and free of opinion and argument or observations which might lead to debate.
3.	Explanations can be sought regarding the intention of the government but not an


explanation of an opinion upon a matter of policy. That is citation 178 in Beauchesne.
4.	Other detailed limitations, some 40 in number, are set out in citation 171 of Beauchesne and apply to oral as well as written questions.
5.	Supplementary questions are matters of grace; that is, at this stage of the proceedings.
6.	The minister is entitled to notice if he asks for it. An answer cannot be insisted upon nor is it regular to comment upon refusal to answer. In effect oral questions are a limited supplement to the questions which may be put on the order paper, and are for the purpose of enabling hon. members to get information on public affairs of urgent importance without delay and to bring such matters to the attention of the government.
As I said, I am not reflecting upon anything that has been done nor commenting upon any particular episode, but in accordance with what seemed to me to be good custom of former Speakers I draw these practices-because they are practices rather than specific provisions in the rules-to the attention of hon. members for their guidance so that we can make the best use of our time and particularly not unduly extend the period of routine proceedings.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, January 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Emilien Morissette for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, hon. members will appreciate that a speech which has had to be broken off is not altogether easy to resume without making a summary of what has already been said. However, I do not propose to follow the usual course of reviewing in any detail what I said previously or of repeating the views which I expressed on behalf of the Canadian government regarding nuclear weapons. Those views are fully set forth at 79951-0-10
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker page 73 of Hansard. I will content myself by simply summarizing what has already been said with regard to the lack of certainty, and confusion referred to in the amendment, and the examples which I gave respecting the views expressed in various parts of Canada and the United States by the Leader of the Opposition. During the intervening months since last session, he indicated fully the degree of the confusion of his views and the uncertainty of his remedies in this particular matter.
Much has been made today of some remarks passed last evening on the national television network to which I am making no reference, a full answer having been given. I know the hon. Leader of the Opposition will recall that he, too, had an experience on November 10, 1959 when, in a press conference, he revealed in some detail his views with regard to various matters, including nuclear weapons. I do not want to be forced into a position where I shall have to go into detail in that regard. But I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that if he would reread the record of that occasion he would, I am sure, come objectively to the conclusion that on the basis of the answers which he gave there was that uncertainty and that confusion which he has included in the motion of non-confidence and ascribed to the government. To summarize what he had to say, without going into detail, he said at page 5 of the text:
We should not get into the field of atomic weapons at all unless we have control over the atomic weapons our forces would be using.
Then, at the bottom of page 6, I quote again:
I said that we should have nothing whatsoever to do with strategic nuclear weapons, the hydrogen bomb, and that sort of thing. We should not allow our forces to use those weapons, however technical they may be and for defence, until we get specific information on the effect they would have on fallout and the atmosphere. I have said we should not allow our forces to be armed by nuclear weapons, tactical or strategical, which are under the control of another power.
Then, a little later on, he had this to say:
We have never been told why the United States should not allow nuclear weapons in the hands of Canadian troops to be under the control of Canadian troops.
And, again:
Are we on the same plane of equipment with the United States forces if a Canadian platoon with a nuclear mortar cannot use it except on orders from the United States forces.
It was in order to answer such uncertainty and confusion in the mind of the hon. gentleman that I went particularly into detail, because the views of the government have been expressed on more than one occasion by the Minister of National Defence. Indeed I would

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker point out that on November 17-and I am referring to a report by Clark Davey, a Globe and Mail reporter-appeared the following:
Liberal Leader Pearson predicted today-
That would be November 16.
-that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization would find itself in serious trouble unless the United States, Britain and Prance dedicated control of their nuclear weapons to the NATO council in every circumstance short of total war.
I think the answer to the ideas expressed by the hon. gentleman were given by himself the other day in silence when I asked him what he would do were he to find out that it would be impossible to secure the consent of all 15 countries. What, then, would his actions be?
Then the report goes on to say:
In a 70-minute press conference which seemed to confuse Liberal defence policy as often as it clarified it, Mr. Pearson returned to his argument that Canadian forces should not be armed with nuclear weapons under the control of any other country. He came close to calling for the scrapping of Canada's nine home defence squadrons of CF-lOO's because they were obsolete, but never took what appeared to be his thinking out loud quite that far.
And then the article goes on-this is a quotation again:
No one power, no matter how powerful, should have authority, within the NATO alliance to approve the use of nuclear weapons on its own.
Then, a little later:
There was more than national pride involved, he added. It was a case of national sovereignty. He suggested it might be better to move United States forces into Canadian bases under a political agreement between the two countries, and permit them to fire as well as control nuclear weapons.
And finally, amidst this series of statements characterized by that confusion and uncertainty which is incorporated in the amendment, we have the hon. gentleman saying this:
The Canadian forces and the Canadian government-would be in a much stronger position if Canada bought its own missiles.
That was on November 16, 1959. A few days later the hon. gentleman went to Halifax and as reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, he said:
I do not think Canada should accept nuclear weapons either under our own or any other control until we know a great deal more about the effects of radiation.
That is an unusually uncertain course and view to be expressed by one who says that this government, having made its position clear, is uncertain.
Let me pass on to the next report, taken from the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of November 24, which comments on a statement made by the hon. gentleman:

Addressing a packed assembly in the spacious Donald Eddy memorial hall here, he said the Liberal party "will vigorously oppose the decision of Prime Minister Diefenbaker's government to equip Canadian forces with weapons that can be used for the defence of Canada only with the authority of another country."
-The United States was a friendly power but nevertheless it was not right that "a single country should control the defence of another."
The next report is taken from the Winnipeg Free Press and I know the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will appreciate this. It carries the headline: "Haggis Puts Mike in Mood". The article states:
"Intolerable" was the word Mr. Pearson used to describe the situation where at Canadian missile sites an American must press the button to send off a Bomarc missile. Canadian forces should not be armed with any form of nuclear weapon the use of which is controlled by any other single government.
What basis did the hon. gentleman have for all these statements? Surely not the declarations made by the Minister of National Defence. Let us examine what was said by the minister. It is not a case of my having just one newspaper report because there are many and they are consistent. The Ottawa Citizen on November 10, 1959, reported:
Canada will have atomic warheads for the Bomarc missiles by 1961, defence minister Pearkes indicated today. He rejected the suggestion that United States officers would control Canadian Bomarc atomic warheads. Mr. Pearkes emphasized that the Bomarc was a defensive weapon. Under no circumstances could this atomic weapon be used without the express consent of the Canadian government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And that of the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This is the surprising thing in this connection, Mr. Speaker, that on a matter as serious as survival the Leader of the Opposition, knowing that these statements had been made by the Minister of National Defence reflecting the views of the government, proceeded to carry across Canada the message that the use in Canada of nuclear weapons, if they were brought into Canada, would be at the wish, authority and under the control of another power.
I quote from an article which appeared in the Toronto Star written by William McGuffin, staff writer:
Mr. Pearkes emphasized-
Referring to the weapons in question:
-that they "cannot be used without the permission of the Canadian government."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Of course, they are our
weapons.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is what the record

I go back to the days of Nehemiah. He followed that course; he maintained his defences and at the same time continued to press for action and agreement to attain peace.
There is one matter to which some reference has been made on other occasions. It was not made by the hon. gentleman the other day. I refer to the question of nuclear testing. The important test of the prospects for successful negotiations will be the success or failure of the resumed negotiations on nuclear testing. In the weeks between now and the middle of May there will be renewed opportunities for the representatives of the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union who have been meeting at Geneva for the past months to make further progress toward agreement on the discontinuance of nuclear tests. I have on many occasions emphasized the importance which the Canadian government attaches to the successful outcome of those negotiations. The achievement of a treaty on nuclear testing, apart from the new confidence that it would build up and bring to the later talks on general disarmament would be of value as evidence of the practicability of joint measures of inspection and control. Moreover, as my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs made clear at the recent session of the general assembly, the Canadian government hopes that there will be an end to nuclear testing.

I pointed out the development of the aircraft had been a success, although behind the original schedule. Then, I used these words.
Unfortunately these outstanding achievements have been overtaken by events. In recent months it has come to be realized that the bomber threat against which the CF-105 was intended to provide defence has diminished, and alternative means of meeting the threat have been developed much earlier than was expected.

I set out in some detail the necessity of action being taken to assure that Canada's expenditure should return the largest possible degree of potential defence. I pointed out that there had been a change in the international outlook and that throughout the year, on more than one occasion, the minister of defence has referred in detail to that changing concept. He does not say it is taking place today but it is under way.
The change from the manned bomber to the intercontinental ballistic missile and other tactical weapons is accelerating. There were many who thought that he was unjustified in this regard. I mentioned the other day the speech made by Mr. Khrushchev and I am going to refer to his exact words on this subject for these words bear out the intelligence that was available to the Canadian government that there was a change taking place and that the U.S.S.R. was reducing the number of manned bombers and more and more directing its attention to intercontinental and other missiles. I am referring now to a verbatim report of his speech. Mr. Khrushchev said:
Our state has at its disposal powerful rocket equipment. The military air force and navy have lost their previous importance in view of the modern development of military equipment. This type of armament is not being reduced but replaced. Almost the entire military air force is being replaced by rocket equipment. We have by now sharply cut, and it seems will continue sharply to cut and even discontinue the manufacture of bombers and other obsolete equipment. In the navy, the submarine fleet assumes great importance, while surface ships can no longer play the part they once did. In our country the armed forces have been to a considerable extent transferred to rocket and nuclear arms. These arms are being perfected and will continue to be perfected until they are banned.
There is no doubt whatsoever that we realized the effect of the decision which we had to make in February of 1959 but, having regard to the knowledge we had, in all honour we could take no other. We were criticized severely for the stand we took at that time in respect of the CF-105. In the light of events that have taken place since, that decision was a proper decision. It was not based, as one weekly magazine recently said, on any direction on the part of the Prime Minister, and so there will be no mistake about it let me say that it was Time magazine. That decision was based on the unified agreement of the cabinet as a whole arrived at as a result of representations from those who had some knowledge of what was going on in the U.S.S.R. I emphasize that fact. It was a decision that all of us would have been pleased not to make. We would have been pleased if we

One night I raised a question, and in the days of war we were extremely careful not to raise anything that in any way might cause doubts on the unity of the country as a whole or might undermine confidence anywhere in our defence policies. I pointed out that in so far as the air force training schemes were concerned-the elementary flying training schools-large profits were being made by private people operating them. I remember Hon. Mr. Power rising and saying there was no foundation for that statement, and he did so with power and effect. I knew the statement was correct. I said, "If the minister finds that I am right, will he change the situation?" I shall always remember the next morning when he called me on the telephone and said, "You were right and it will be stopped". That man is today in the Senate. In the days of war-it is not too late to pay a tribute to him; and in doing so I am not taking away any honour from the other ministers of defence-he made a tremendous contribution to Canada.

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker It is extremely difficult for that scrutiny and supervision to be carried out in a house composed of as many members as we have here; and I believe that if a committee on expenditure were set up, with an appropriate reference which could be agreed upon by the leaders of the government and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), much good would result.
I think those were appropriate words. This matter has been fully discussed. I point out the tremendous responsibility resting on those who must discharge the duties of government, in determining what course to follow, not to be dominated by the military-the civil authority must be supreme-but to secure from the military and other qualified persons, both within our own country and outside of it, the best information we can obtain and then, having secured that information to act, whatever the detrimental political consequences may be.
I am therefore going to advise the house that it is my intention to move for the setting up of a special select committee on defence expenditures. The Leader of the Opposition has suggested that it should be a small committee. I am prepared to accept, as is the government, the views of hon. members in this house as to the numbers in that committee, to the end that there will be available a body which will determine the course it will take as to what meetings shall or shall not be open or closed. But in the light of all the circumstances, it will review the expenditures to the end that the ability, the training and the capacity of members in every part of the house may be used for the purpose of examining this most important problem.
There has been some criticism that some of these things have not been mentioned in the speech from the throne.
