I wonder if the Prime
Minister will tell us in what publication these figures will be found?
Certainly. By looking up the records.
What records?
The records of the Department of Defence Production. I have already given that information.
Which publication of the department?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Unless the hon. member has the floor he has not the right to press his questions.
Is it not customary, when figures have been cited by the Prime Minister, to identify the source?
Where did you get them?
I was not speaking in the House of Commons, and I got my own figures.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not going to say it is not customary for a speaker using figures to give the source-
I have nothing more to add, excepting this: that last remark of the Leader of the Opposition reveals the situation-"I did not use those figures in the House of Commons".
I used them and I identified them, which is more than you did.
They were given on the national television and they bore no resemblance to the facts.
Prime ministerial infallibility. This is the truth.

I am sorry to have taken the length of time I have but I felt it necessary to deal with the question of defence which was dealt with at such length by the Leader of the Opposition.
I am going to deal now as briefly as I can with the general state of the economy. I propose to do so because last year the hon. member for Essex East who is a skilled parliamentarian indicated that I had failed to refer to Canada's financial situation in the throne speech debate. I shall leave the various specialized fields of governmental activity to the respective ministers who will report on the situation in the fields under their purview and I shall leave it to the Minister of Finance to make a detailed statement concerning the monetary and fiscal front. I am simply going to refer for a few moments to the forebodings and predictions of catastrophe and calamity, the chronic wails and

the repetitious use of words such as "fumbling" that were indulged in by the Leader of the Opposition.
This word "fumbling" is an interesting one and apparently it holds a peculiar fascination for that hon. gentleman. He even used it with reference to the United Kingdom, France and the United States. They fumbled, too, he said, as reported in a speech in Geneva Park on August 10, 1958. Let me put it in the kindliest way: his overuse of the word seems to indicate a marked tendency to a jaundiced view of things.
Hon. members will have noticed that he stayed away from the specialized field of prophecy when he spoke the other day. There was a reference to boom in his speech. He stayed away from a discussion of what happened in 1959 as compared to what he predicted would happen. Look at the record. His prophecies of January, 1959, viewed in the light of retrospect become a calendar of confusion in which he apparently took his counsel from frustration.
"Disaster, financial mess." You have heard those expressions from the hon. gentleman, Mr. Speaker, if you read the press. His 1958 remarks on the throne speech in the house contained dark forebodings couched in terms such as these:-"We are still in the recession." I refer you to pages 25 and 30 of Hansard of that year. Other expressions in which he freely indulged were: "Inflation therefore remains a menace in the midst of recession, that is the dilemma." In 1959 he depicted our future in sombre tones.
It Is the most difficult and dangerous situation that has confronted this country in many years. The economic picture as it faces us in this country today is a picture of recession and unemployment, a picture of inflation and rising prices, becoming more and more dangerous, the government placing an inflationary time bomb in the midst of our national economy.
Last year the hon. gentleman gave expression to this thought:
We may well reach a very dangerous situation, a crisis of confidence, rising prices, rising costs, rising deficits and rising unemployment.
That is the general picture he placed before the people. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) as reported at page 37 of Hansard of January 19, 1959, directed a question to the Leader of the Opposition in these words:
Why do you not offer something constructive, then?
The hon. gentleman replied:
That is your job.
I am not going to engage in a lengthy recital of the statements that were made although I have them here in detail. The Leader of the Opposition last year, as was the case in 1957 and 1958, viewed Canada's

economic condition as a mess with trade gone and markets disappearing and inflation stealing from the average Canadian as never before. It was indeed a frightful picture he presented. He did not say things like that the other day. He looked over at me and said-using words to this effect-"I suppose that the Prime Minister has some statements that he will quote." On January 19, 1959, I said, as reported at page 65 of Hansard of that date:
What we need today Is not the kind of picayune attitude exhibited by the Leader of the Opposition but more hope and less fear ... We on this side of the house have confidence in Canada her present and her future.
What has happened in the intervening time? I am simply going to place before the house in very few words an outline of the economic outlook of our country. Notwithstanding the failure of efforts of hon. members opposite as prophets a year ago, they have recently been expressing concern about the economic outlook for 1960. No one in the world can but have concern today. One has only to read Mr. Khrushchev's speech of a few days ago to realize that he believes the communist system will ultimately destroy capitalism, that the communist system will take over because it can do a better job economically. Over and over again when he spoke in the United States Mr. Khrushchev told the industrialists of that country that when he said, "I will bury you." What he meant was not burial with bombs but with improved economic prospects under a communist regime.
A realistic appraisal of Canada's economic prospects for 1960 requires that all these problems be seen in their proper perspective. I have examined the situation in particular this year to ascertain what has transpired since the house met in January of 1959. Canada's gross national product in 1959 is estimated at about $34,750 million, an increase of 7 per cent as forecast in the budget by the Minister of Finance. Since the 1959 over-all price level was on the average about 2 per cent above that of 1958, the gain in national output in volume terms was about 5 per cent. Both in value and dollar terms, Canada produced more goods and services in 1959 than in any other year in history.
During the first 11 months of 1959 the number of persons with jobs averaged 5,880,000 representing 2.7 per cent more than the 5,726,000 average for the corresponding period of 1958. Unemployment throughout the year was lower than in 1958.
Much was said by hon. gentlemen opposite about the danger of exports and how we were losing our trade. Canada's exports of goods in 1959 exceeded the $5 billion mark for
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker the first time. This record high level of commodity exports is about 5 per cent above both the 1958 level and the previous peak of 1957, and that in a world where trading blocs are being established as the Leader of the Opposition said and at a time when Mr. Khrushchev pictures an all-out communist world economic offensive. This is a record not unworthy of Canada.
Capital spending by business after a two year decline commenced to turn upward in the second quarter of 1959 and has been rising ever since.
They spoke of runaway inflation. The consumer price index averaged 1.1 per cent higher in 1959 than in 1958. There is a renewed confidence in government securities, the particulars of which I could give but which will be given by the Minister of Finance.
The government's general financial policy has been criticized by the hon. gentleman. He talks of the largest cash deficit in history, the largest addition ever made to the national debt. These statements on his part are not supported by the facts. Government expenditures in relation to the gross national product in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1960 are estimated at about 16 per cent of the gross national product. That is about approximately the same proportion as total federal government expenditures to gross national product for the three years from 1955 to 1957. On the basis of net national debt in relation to gross national product, the relation of the net national debt per capita, in both of these there is a clear expression of a strong financial position in Canada.
We made expenditures. We expanded the housing developments of Canada; we extended social security; we made more available to the provinces than ever before, and more public works, as the Minister of Finance says, than ever before.
Twice as much for coal.

We did these things in order to meet a situation where Canada found itself in a recession, a recession that was joined in by the United States. We fought the recession; we met the situation. As a result of our action many extensions in social security payments were made. It is all very well for the opposition to say that these things we did while in office. Well, they made provision for hospital insurance, but we had to put up the money, $160 million.

The taxpayers put up the money.
148	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker

We did not increase the amount of family allowance payments but the number of families increased the annual amount by $98 million. In fact, there was about half a billion dollars increase in the expenditures in social security; old age pensions and the federal government's share of assistance to the blind, disabled and unemployed increased by $38 million. Payments of pensions and other benefits to war veter -[DOT] ans increased by $34 million. I could go on. There was extra assistance provided to the provinces. All of these things we have to do, many of these things we have to do; many of them were necessary to meet the recession situation.
I ask whoever follows me to tell me this: Is it wasteful to spend more money to fight recession? Is it wasteful to bring social assistance to additional Canadians? Is it wasteful to provide more funds for the provinces and municipalities? Is it wasteful to spend money to further national development? These are some of the kinds of expenditures that were made, all of which were necessary to meet a situation. In so far as the national development plan is concerned, it has brought about new vistas of development in this country. Indeed, on the occasion of the Liberal meeting in the month of December the Hon. George Prudham paid tribute to what had been done by this government in northern development, a development that should have taken place years before as I see it and as this government sees it.
Now, then, last year-and I notice the Leader of the Opposition did not get around to this part of the speech this year-the chief lieutenant of the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Essex East, quoted what the bank presidents had to say. I would like to hear them quote today the views expressed across Canada by the very presidents and general managers to whom the hon. member for Essex East referred last year as being critical of this government and of Canadian development and of Canada's economic future. Let me quote from the annual report of the president and general manager of the Toronto-Dominion Bank. This gentleman was mentioned last year at page 185 of Hansard as one of those who was critical of the government; he was mentioned by the hon. member for Essex East. Mr. Ashforth said:
Let us now turn to the Canadian scene.
Canadians in 1959 produced more, imported more, exported more, earned more, spent more and saved more than any previous year.
Last year this gentleman was taken as a witness. This year he was not quoted by the opposition. He went on:
A year ago Canada was labouring in the early stages of recovery from recession. Today, we are


in the midst of a period of broad expansion which is carrying our national output and our standard of living to new heights.
You understand why he was not quoted. What about the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce? What did he have to say in his report:
We may now anticipate in this year a greater production of goods and services than we have experienced in any peacetime period.
Those are the words of Neil McKinnon. He referred to the question of unemployment as it was in September and said:
In September, less than 3 per cent of the labour force was unemployed which, allowing for temporary unemployed and the unemployable, is considered to be full employment.
Then, we have the president of the Imperial Bank, Mr. Proctor. This is his report:
The vigour of the business recovery which was already evident at our last annual meeting, is the most important development of the past year. Last July industrial production stood 8.5 per cent above the recession low of August, 1958, which carried us 2.3 per cent above the peak level of the 1956-57 boom. The rise of 7.5 per cent in gross national product over the last year was almost all solid gain as prices rose only 2 per cent. Employment is now running higher than ever before and unemployment has fallen to much lower levels. Canadians are better off than they have ever been.
Will the Prime Minister permit a question?
Yes.
Was that 1956-57 boom to which the minister referred the recession the government inherited from the Liberals?

As a matter of fact I
could answer that with some of the documents that I have if I could locate them. I can't always find them.
They are hidden again, are they?

Mr. Speaker, the only
time that anything has ever been hidden was the report that was revealed on January 14, 1958, in this house, to the eternal discredit of those who sit opposite.
Mr. Proctor went on to say this, because I believe in calling as witnesses those who the members in the opposition said last year-and I refer particularly to the hon. member for Essex East-were men whose views could be depended upon.
Mr. Proctor went on to say:
That the decline of 1957-1958 was not more drastic is quite remarkable as deflationary forces then at work in the economy were powerful indeed. Inventory investment fell from a 1956 peak rate of $1,100 million a year to a disinvestment rate of $300 million a year at the low point of 1958, a net swing of nearly $2 billion. From peak to trough the change in the annual rate of spending on machinery and equipment amounted to

$800 million and on non-residential construction to $500 million. Yet despite these severe cuts in market demand, gross national expenditure merely paused in its upward march.
The forces sustaining the economy and so accounting for this remarkable behaviour-
I underline these words.
-of the national output in the face of the decline in investment standing are readily identified.
I could go on and take other bank reports one after the other but I will end by quoting from the Financial Post of November 28, 1959 an article headed "They've No Doubts About 1960":
To a sizable cross-section of top Canadian executives, the prospects for business next year look bright indeed. Most expect their companies will chalk up very substantial sales gains in 1960. In a majority of firms, profits will rise appreciably.
It goes on to set out in detail what has been done in this connection. There is the picture, Mr. Speaker, the picture described in the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition in the words set forth there. We have had economic difficulties. In the United States they find that bond prices have fallen to unheard of levels over a period of 25 to 30 years. Interest rates are the highest in 25 years and more. That is the situation in the United States.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, is it the responsibility of the government of Canada that this condition of affairs has arisen? The same situation prevails with respect to interest rates in European countries. Yet the opposition continually harps on these things and endeavours to lead the Canadian people to believe that we are responsible for what has happened with respect to interest rates and the like which are the subject of their criticism. With maximum exports abroad, with the gross national product at the level of which I have spoken, for those things they say that providence is responsible. As the Minister of Finance has said, the level of interest rates is in part due to the increasing demand for investment money in our country.
We are going to meet and face up to these problems which are placed before the people of Canada as our responsibility. When I look at the situation in which we found ourselves after we came into power, having to meet a recession with respect to which the last government concealed the report on Canada's economic outlook-that still seres the heart of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate

with that report hidden from the Canadian people and no action taken on it by the government of the day, with the warnings in that report not having been heeded, none the less we faced up to the situation.

You did not discover it for six months.
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
What is the babbling interruption?
I will tell the Prime Minister what it is. The Prime Minister was in office for six months and did not even find out what was happening.
It was too well hidden.
Does the hon. member say that I did not find the report for six months?
You did not find out what was happening for six months.
He is correct that the report was well hidden.
You did not find out what was happening for six months.

After all, there is the record. There are other matters that will be dealt with that will be equally unpalatable to the opposition. I now read the motion of non-confidence:
This house is of the opinion that the failure of the government to develop and enunciate clear and consistent policies-
I have mentioned some of the clear and consistent policies of the. opposition with respect to defence and some of the clear and consistent prophecies made last year by the opposition.
-or to provide full and accurate information-
Whatever support there is for that I do not know. We have endeavoured to supply accurate information. I have taken today the information supplied by the bank presidents who last year were called as witnesses for the opposition.
-is a major cause of the confusion and uncertainty that prevails about national defence-
Confusion? Uncertainty? Read Hansard, Mr. Speaker. Read the course taken by the Leader of the Opposition on the question of defence. You cannot make sense out of it. It has no directness. It lacks cohesiveness. One statement jars with another, and that is one of the major problems we face.
-public finance, agriculture, markets, employment and in other important areas of governmental responsibility.
The ministers responsible for the particular fields in question will deal therewith. Under all the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, having regard to the fact that even the Leader of the Opposition had to admit there was a boom although he did so with difficulty in view of his prophecies of dire disaster last year and the year before-
May I ask the Prime Minister to point out where I admitted in my speech that there was a boom?

Oh, I cannot find it now.

The Address-Mr. Argue
You certainly cannot; it is not there.
Did the hon. gentleman never use the word "boom"?
I used it but I did not use it in that sense.
Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime
Minister has stated that I said in my speech that there was a boom. This is a point of order, Mr. Speaker-

Apparently the hon.
gentleman did not use the word "boom" in the way I took it but if this is their idea of a boom then I ask the house to interpret "boom" the way the average Canadian does today and to vote confidence in the government.

Mr. Speaker, in recent hours we have seen an exhibition by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) that I suggest does not inspire the confidence and respect of the institution of parliament in him nor will that kind of exhibition likely inspire confidence in him on the part of the Canadian people.
Before going on with the remarks I have to make I should like to compliment the mover of the address (Mr. Morissette). I was extremely sorry that a longstanding engagement, for the first time since I have been a member of the house, made it impossible for me to be here to listen to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. However, from reading the speech, from reports from my colleagues and reports in the press, I know he made an excellent contribution. I am certain that he has more valuable work to perform in the days ahead. I want to agree with all those who have referred to the ability, grace and charm of the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman). We hope she will do the house the honour in the future of rewarding us with many more excellent contributions to our debates.
In his speech the other night the Prime Minister made a number of important announcements and in his speech this afternoon he made the important announcement that a defence committee would be set up.
In reading over the speech from the throne, we find it to be a relatively barren and empty document. I want to associate myself and the C.C.F. party with the remarks made by the Prime Minister about our Governor General and the excellent and competent manner in which he is performing his duties. However, in the speech from the throne which he provided for the Governor General to

read I think the Prime Minister left him very little ammunition because he retained most of it for himself to be used on Monday evening and again today.
We are facing at this time, in my opinion and that of the C.C.F. group, a very great challenge. Our economic system-yes, our way of life-is being challenged today as it has never been challenged before. In the statement of the Prime Minister or in the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) I do not find anything which would indicate to me that they realize the great gravity of this challenge.
The other night the Prime Minister made the announcement that a Hoover commission would be set up to inquire into government efficiency. We shall support any step that is likely to improve the efficiency of government. However, it seems to me that it would be a mistake for the government to spend too much of its energy in endeavouring to ferret out all possible inefficiency and waste and not spend sufficient energy in laying plans for a great economic expansion and development in this country. I think one can be overly concerned with a reduction of expenditures in a period of time when increased expenditures and development are necessary.
We are to have a Hoover commission apparently to look into the efficiency of the civil service. I believe the Canadian civil service is efficient. I believe the government soon-immediately, now-should announce increases in civil service salaries. The civil servants of this country should not be made the victims of the government's failure to halt inflation and to prevent the cost of living from rising. As our production increases, I feel the civil servants have a just claim for a fair share of that increased production. 1 think it would increase the efficiency and the morale of the civil service if the government now dealt with their well founded submissions for certain increases in salary.
I do not believe the people of Canada or of the North American continent are prepared to accept the position of second-class world citizens. As we look forward to celebrating the one hundredth anniversary of this country we should be taking every feasible step to make certain that the wealth and the production of this nation expands at the greatest possible rate and that such production is made available to Canadians and is distributed on an equitable basis.
I never thought that I would see the time in this house when the statements of the premier of the Soviet union would be quoted by the Prime Minister of the country in support of action taken by the government. People are coming to realize that statements

made by that gentleman and statistics emanating from that country are such that they should be given our greatest consideration.
I think there are many aspects of our capitalistic system that can be questioned. Unless some of the difficulties and some of the crises that face our nation are overcome we may well become second-class world citizens in this decade. Soviet production is going ahead at an exceedingly rapid rate. It is forecast that by 1965 its industrial production will overtake that of the United States.
The joint Canadian-United States committee recently issued a publication entitled "The Growth of Soviet Economic Power" in which it is pointed out that the industrial capacity of the Soviet union is increasing at the rate of 9.5 per cent per year as compared to an increase of 3.5 per cent in the United States. Although per capita consumption in the Soviet union is low, it is expanding at the rate of 5 per cent per year as compared to a rate of increase of only 3 per cent in Canada and the United States.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Could he identify the source of the information? I was not quite sure I heard it correctly.

It is a book entitled "The Growth of Soviet Economic Power" put out by the well known joint Canadian-United States committee, an official committee between Canada and the United States. I do not think anybody is going to question the validity of the members of that committee or their importance or the statistics that I have just quoted from their publication.
In my opinion the first thing that our nation needs to look to is this tremendous lag in production. Production may have gone up some, as it has, this year. It may level off next year. There may be a recession in the following year, a matter about which I shall have something more to say.
The second reason we need to look at this economic system is that we have been wasting our resources. We have unemployed resources in the maritime provinces. We have unemployed resources in the agricultural industry. Agricultural producers are facing grave marketing difficulties. The government's program of deficiency payments is not working out. The agricultural industry is not receiving its fair share of the income of this country. Its production is not as efficient as it could be and the best possible use of that production is not being made.
The Address-Mr. Argue
Another way in which our economy is wasteful is in the field of defence expenditures. There is a private member's resolution on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), which sets forth the opinion and the policy of the C.C.F. with regard to defence and defence questions. I am not going to read that resolution at this time because my time is limited and time does not permit. We believe that there is room for a substantial reduction in the defence expenditures of this country. We think that not only did the previous administration spend money on defence that was proven a waste, but that this government is doing the very same thing. For example, we think that the Bomarc will be proven to be a waste of money and an inconsequential addition to Canada's defence.
We welcome the setting up of a defence committee. Not only do we welcome the setting up of such a committee, but we suggest to the Prime Minister that a member of the opposition might be made the chairman of that committee, and that the committee should not only examine defence expenditures but should look at defence policy and arrive at the best possible defence policy for the days ahead. There is not much use in inquiring into the mistakes which have been made in the past if the committee is not allowed to set up its own view as to what policy should be followed in the defence matters of this country.
Another way our economy is falling, another area in which we are losing production, is because of unemployment. Recent statistics show that there are 370,000 unplaced applicants for work in this country, or 5.9 per cent of the labour force. Surely this is an indictment of this system when almost 6 per cent of our man power and woman power-and this is a growing percentage-should be unemployed and should not have the opportunity to perform useful work.
We are experiencing other difficulties. We are experiencing a trade crisis. The government can talk of increased exports, but we are all aware that Canada's export markets are in jeopardy, that many of Canada's industries are finding difficulty in obtaining markets.
I would like to refer, Mr. Speaker, to the report of the Canadian-United States joint committee on the growth of Soviet economic power, in which it points out that Canadian exports of lumber to the United Kingdom have declined substantially since 1954-55 from over $70 million at that time to not much over $40 million in 1958, while Russian exports have continued to rise more or less

The Address-Mr. Argue steadily. In fact, since 1956 United Kingdom imports of lumber from Russia have consistently exceeded those from Canada.
As far as wheat is concerned, the Soviet union has now become the world's third largest wheat exporting nation and it is forecast that Russia will be able by 1965 to export from five million to ten million tons of wheat, which will endanger Canada's position as the second largest wheat exporting nation. This is an economic offensive; this is an economic threat to the welfare of Canada, and something about which the government needs to develop a new and farsighted trade policy.
Mr. Speaker, may I-

Mr. Speaker, I have only forty minutes, and questions can be put to me after I conclude, at which time I shall be very pleased to answer all of the questions of the hon. gentleman.
This country is facing a trade crisis in another way. Our deficit of international payments is rapidly growing higher. It is estimated that during this year the deficit may exceed more than $1,500 million. This means that to a larger and larger extent the control and ownership of the resources of this country are being transferred to foreign citizens. It means that our country's future is being mortgaged. Therefore we will have to repay these obligations at some future date, and in the meantime a very large part of the productive wealth of this country will accrue to people outside our nation. We heard so much from hon. gentlemen opposite over the years about the domination of Canadian industry by United States capital and about the control of Canadian industry by that capital. We had expected that the government would do something that would at least reduce the rate of transfer of control of Canadian industry to outside capital. That has not happened. Instead of a reduction, the rate has accelerated.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a very eminent Canadian, Mr. J. E. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada, made a very interesting speech in Winnipeg on January 18. The governor of the Bank of Canada is reported by the Winnipeg papers as having stated the following:
Canadian savings and the machinery of the Canadian capital market now can supply all of the capital funds needed by governments and business combined to carry on a capital expenditure program as large in total as is sound and healthy for the Canadian economy to sustain in any one year-


In other words, according to the governor of the Bank of Canada the $1500 million international deficit that this country has incurred is unsound and unhealthy. I think that this is a tremendous indictment of this government by the governor of the Bank of Canada. Action by the government is necessary to reduce Canada's dependence on outside capital and to increase the ownership of Canadian resources by Canadians.
The Prime Minister talked about inflation. He seemed to be quite happy that, in his view, inflation was not serious. But I would suggest that a 2 per cent annual increase in the price level is serious. Over a lifetime it eats away a very substantial part of the savings of the Canadian people. Inflation is a robber of the earnings of low income groups, and is a very great danger which faces this country today. We have a lag in production. We are wasting many of our natural and human resources. A larger and larger part of the industry and wealth of this country is being transferred to outside ownership.
We face inflation, but apparently the problem of recession and depression has not yet been mastered. The Prime Minister referred to conditions today. The year end report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) forecast a relatively prosperous 1960; but the minister and the government have failed to look into the future, and we wonder why they have not made a report of conditions that are likely to occur in 1961 or 1962.
I have in my hand the Winnipeg Free Press of Saturday, January 9, which bears the heading:
Recession in 1962, government expert fears; warns post-war down turn.
Another heading reads: "Could mean election day switch" and it is an article by Victor Mackie, the well-known and competent journalist of the Winnipeg Free Press.
I have since obtained the speech delivered by Dr. O. J. Firestone, the economic adviser in the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I am wondering if he is the author of the so-called hidden report. I ask if he has made the same submission to the minister and to the government as he made to the Canadian people in this well known speech. In that speech he said:
What I am implying is that the recession we may be facing in 1962 could be more extensive than anything we have yet experienced since the end of the second world war.
In other words, unless action is taken to thwart this danger our nation could be facing in 1962 a greater and more serious recession than anything which prevailed under the former Liberal administration. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to reveal

any report he has from his economic experts forecasting economic conditions in Canada in 1961 and 1962. The nation should be apprised now of the possibility of a depression or a severe recession in 1962. We cannot compete with the growing production of the Soviet union and the threat which it presents to democracy and to our type of system if we have to face periodic booms and busts. I see nothing in the economic policy of the government or in the proposals in the speech from the throne-or in the speech by the Leader of the Opposition which lacks proposals- which would suggest to me that there is a program forthcoming which would make possible the increase in production of which our nation is capable. I believe that 1960 will see for all practical purposes the end in this country of many of the basic tenets on which the Liberal and Conservative parties are founded with respect to our economic system and our so-called free enterprise economy.
One of the things we have in common in all parts of this house is a belief in democracy, a belief in the importance of free discussion, a belief that the ordinary citizen should have a right to the facts. But I wonder if the ordinary citizen of this country today has access to the facts, or if the millions of dollars which are used by advertisers learning from the Madison avenue mass media manipulators have so influenced the judgment of the Canadian people as to make it impossible for many citizens to exercise a free, fair and unbiased judgment. The government is turning increasingly the television and radio facilities of this country over to private hands; there has been a very disturbing growth in newspaper chains across this country until today four groups control approximately one third of the circulation of all the newspapers in Canada. Is this something which is in keeping with democracy and in keeping with free discussion?
I think this represents a great danger to freedom and to democracy and I think we should inquire into what effective steps can be taken to break the monopoly which exists in these media and whether we can reduce the quantity of advertising, so that freedom of will will not be in jeopardy. I do not know what the answers may be, but I have placed this resolution on the order paper and I am pleased that in this members' lottery instituted by the government in which all the resolutions are put into a hat and drawn, mine is in such a position that it is likely to be debated. I am hopeful we can set up a committee of this house to inquire into the whole question of the control of newspaper, radio and television facilities in this country so that all feasible and practical steps may be
The Address-Mr. Argue taken which will assure freedom of discussion and maintenance of the strength of democracy in Canada.
Here are some of the problems which face our nation. Here are some of the challenges, and I suggest that there are certain things which should be done at this time. The first thing which I suggest is that we should agree that there is a sense of urgency, that we cannot delay throughout this decade in coming to grips with the problem of lagging production and the need to accelerate production. We should come to grips with the problem of unused and underemployed resources. We in the C.C.F. say we need a national economic plan; that there should be some direction of the economy by the government in order that there may be a channelling of investment into the most productive fields and the most necessary industries. We say that there should be at this time a further development of social security measures; that the great productive capacity of this country should be made available to the people of the nation. We say that there should be an increase in old age pensions brought into effect at this session. To ask senior citizens of this country to exist on $55 a month is not in keeping with our concept of democracy and justice. The pension should be at least $75 a month.
We suggest that the government's hospitalization program, which has been so well accepted across this country in almost every province and will be accepted soon, we hope, in all the provinces, should be still further developed. It is time, in our view, for another great step forward during this session and for the government to introduce an over-all medical plan which will make it possible for provinces to provide medical, dental and optical services. The province of Saskatchewan, under our C.C.F. government, in 1947 pioneered in the field of hospitalization. I am confident that Saskatchewan will pioneer again in the field of prepaid medical services by re-electing the present government and thereby assuring the people of that province the beginning of a pre-paid medical program on January 1, 1961.
We say that there is a need for a further development of public ownership. When I read some of the debates and some of the controversy which is going on within the British labour party today, I think there are people in that party who are walking into a trap which has been set for them by political enemies. I think that an increasing development of public ownership is necessary. I have already advocated some increase in the field of health insurance. I wish I had time to refer as I would like to to the last annual report of Trans-Canada Air Lines

The Address-Mr. Argue which I have on my desk in which it is indicated there has been a reduction of 20 per cent in tourist fares. The president of the company said that in 1959, if it had not been for Canadian Pacific Air Lines and the inefficient duplication of services allowed by the government of Canada Trans-Canada Air Lines could have brought about another 5 per cent reduction in fares. This is an indication of efficiency in public service.
The Saskatchewan government insurance office in a competitive way, without any control over the purchasers of insurance, has brought down fire insurance rates on home dwellings in Saskatchewan to a rate of 40 cents per $100 of insurance as compared to 70 cents in either Alberta or Manitoba.
There is room for a further development of public ownership. I am not suggesting all out nationalization or that the government should move in and confiscate industry. I am fully opposed to such a move but in a growing and expanding economy, in the interests of efficiency and lower prices, there is room for an expansion of public ownership as well as of the co-operative movement. There is also room for private enterprise and for the individual businessman. But as the price spreads commission report pointed out, in the food retailing industry the independent merchant is being squeezed to the wall. The people who are true free enterprisers are going out of existence under the policies followed by this government. There is room for corporate ownership, too, but that should be controlled and it also needs to be developed in the interests of Canadians.
We suggest there is need for management in the field of trade, that if Mr. Coyne is right in saying that in relation to other factors we can produce the capital required for development in this country without depending on outside capital to the extent of $1,500 million, steps should be taken to develop the Canadian economy in the interests of Canadians.
We feel that under the system of trade and with increased tariffs the international payments situation is not likely to improve. We think our movement in the years ahead has an opportunity to be of great service to the people of this country. We do not feel as our opponents often tell us that there is a great division in the interests of farmers, workers, small businessmen and professional people. As we see it, the people in this country who are prepared and willing to engage in productive services should have an opportunity to receive a fair return for their services.
We think there is need for a greater measure of equality. We feel we must play our role in international affairs as Canadians. Not

only should we be producing more goods in Canada and making these available, on a more equitable basis to Canadian citizens but we should be prepared to play an increasing part in making our production available to underdeveloped countries and needy nations throughout the world.
We need in this country a bill of rights without question, but we need one that is not simply window dressing. We need a bill of rights of substance, one that guarantees fundamental human freedoms for the people of Canada. We feel that such a bill of rights, should be properly an amendment to the constitution. The Prime Minister has announced that steps are being taken to meet the situation in a certain way and we feel he should consider a bill of rights as an amendment to the constitution.
Believing that our economy has been wasteful and that there is need for the government to remove uncertainty and confusion, I should like to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom the period after the word "responsibility" and adding thereto the following words:
"and has failed to initiate the fundamental economic and social planning necessary to remove the uncertainty and confusion that exists."
We feel it is imperative for the Canadian nation to realize the challenge that exists from abroad, to accept that challenge, and to so order our economy so as to make the great wealth of this nation available to all our citizens.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? I believe that the hon. member for Assiniboia referred the house to statistics on trade from which he quoted and indicated that they were issued by an official joint committee of Canada and the United States. Could he elaborate further and tell the house in what way this committee is an official committee?

Mr. Speaker, I do not believe it is a governmental committee but I think it was composed of officials of this country who are well known. The president of the Canadian Labour Congress comes to mind as well as the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and some well known economists in the government service. This is a joint committee of Canadian and United States citizens. The committee is composed of highly respected persons who are doing a survey in various economic matters of mutual interest. I think this is a very fine document that has been produced and that the members of this committee are responsible individuals. T believe this publication should recommend itself to the hon. member.

(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I want to tender the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) my most sincere congratulations for his magnificent contribution in answer to the speech from the throne. I also want to add a tribute to our colleague, the hon. member for the riding of Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman).
If other hon. members who will take part in the present discussion give us contributions equal in quality to those of the hon. members for Rimouski and Grenville-Dundas, I am sure that the whole debate on the speech from the throne will be not only most interesting but also very useful.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, the members of this house who have the interests of their country and its people at heart must surely have derived encouragement from the indicators brought to our attention by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) which demonstrated the buoyant condition of the economy of our country today. On January 11, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when speaking in Toronto to the Canadian Club, said this:
For the Canadian economy, the new decade of the 1960's opens in an expansionary phase, one that gives promise of being more securely founded in terms of demand, resources and productivity. Nineteen sixty offers the prospect of continued sustainable growth provided we are prepared to pay heed to the lessons of the 1950's. New elements bid fair to come forward to lift the economy to new heights, chief among them export demand and capital investment.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) in a statement he issued from his office in Ottawa on December 28, spoke with equal optimism about the future. He pointed out in his statement that whereas Canada's expansion at the beginning of the last decade got its stimulus from defence, from our involvement in the Korean war, and the assistance given to the inauguration of NATO, today's expansion at the beginning of the 1960's was, as he put it, "anchored to the more solid foundations of constructive peacetime pursuits". He emphasized that the present dominant push comes from the growing needs of Canadians for goods and services. Our economic recovery and our present expansion run alongside the economy of the United States.
Notwithstanding the opinions that have been voiced-as were expected-to the contrary, by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the leader of the C.C.F. group, I belong, I think, to that much larger group of fellow Canadians who believe that the present condition in our economy was not
The Address-Mr. Maloney something that was brought about by accident but was brought about as a direct result of government activity commenced on June 21, 1957.
Never in the history of our country has so dedicated a group worked so tirelessly in the interests of their country to restore health to its economy and to restore optimism and confidence to the spirit of our people.
I want to take advantage of the next few minutes to say a few words about the subject of immigration. I have not found at any time any criticism from any reliable quarter about the decision of the government to put into effect a plan, originally decided upon by its Liberal predecessor in 1957, of reducing the number of immigrants admitted to Canada, and of continuing a slowdown policy during a time when it was believed by many that it was neither fair nor just to entice immigrants to come to Canada because of the recessive forces that were then at work in our country, in the United States and in so many countries of the world during parts of 1957 and 1958.

I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit a question. He has made the statement, if I understood it correctly, that the government has continued a policy initiated by their predecessor. Does he refer to something that was done by me? If so, will he tell the house what it was, because I have no recollection of having initiated any policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You never did anything.

I refer, Mr. Speaker, to the plan formulated by the government of which the hon. member was a member and which was introduced to slow down the number of immigrants admitted to Canada, a plan which we did not cause any interference with after the election of June 10.
I deny categorically that there ever was any such plan.

Mr. Speaker, the facts speak for themselves, and I regret I find myself in the position of contradicting my hon. friend.
In view, however, of the statements which have been made about the economy of our country and its condition today by the Prime Minister, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and in view of the comparable good condition of the United States economy, it occurs to me that the time is now ripe to take a second look at the policy which has been in effect since the summer of 1957.
An analysis of the statistics issued by the dominion bureau concerning the numbers and ethnic origin of immigrants from overseas

The Address-Mr. Maloney between the years 1946 and 1957 inclusive shows that in that period we admitted a total of 1,669,340 immigrants, ranging from Albanians to the various people who make up the country of Yugoslavia. Peoples of over 47 different ethnic origins came to Canada in that interval. By far the largest percentage came from England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales. Immigrants from the British Isles totalled 31.9 per cent of the over-all immigration during that period. I was surprised to observe that up to the end of 1957 immigrants from France represented only 2 per cent of our over-all immigration, the numbers being 32,729. I should like to see further encouragement held out to immigrants coming from the motherland of Canada's other great basic race. Immigrants to the number of 12.9 per cent came from Germany; 11.6 per cent from Italy, although this percentage, I would imagine, is somewhat higher now by reason of the additional immigration of large numbers of very worth-while Italian immigrants in the year 1959. In the year 1958 the additional number of immigrants admitted to Canada was 124,700, making a grand total since 1946, and including that year, of approximately 2 million immigrants.
I have heard it estimated that we lose annually to the United States of America something like 40,000 of our residents. If that is so, then the net gain of immigrants over emigrants between the years 1956 and 1959 would have been about 1J million, a loss of about 25 per cent.
It is not uncommon to hear fellow citizens, when we talk about this subject, voice the view that people who are permitted to enter Canada as immigrants take jobs from Canadians already established and aggravate conditions of unemployment in the country. Such people, of course, fail to advert to the contribution that immigrants make by their employment of labour, their consumption of Canadian products and their production of wealth.
Well informed economists who study the subject with the knowledge of experts take the position that these arguments are false and insist that there is little or no connection between immigration and unemployment. The royal commissioners responsible for the report on Canada's economic prospects, after an exhaustive review and study of our country's economy and of the factors that give it health, stated that immigrants have made a decided contribution to the scale of economic development in Canada. In part of their report they state:
It is our firm belief that it is in Canada's interest to continue to encourage people from other countries to emigrate here in order both to assist and

participate in the development of our country and also to contribute further variety to our social organizations and institutions.
Three quarters of the immigrants who come to Canada are adults but only half of them are persons who go into our labour force. The other half are wives or children or dependents who fall into some other category. In other words, it is only the remaining half which takes its place in the labour market and often brings with it badly needed skills.
An illustration of that point can be found with reference to the figures for 1958 when, as I say, about 124,700 immigrants came to Canada. Of this group 30,344 were children, 24,795 were wives and the others who fell into the category of dependents numbered 6,534. The balance, numbering 63,078, included workers of all kinds broken up into a number of different categories, many of whom intended to get into the field of manufacturing or construction or on some kind of project where mechanical skill would be required.
Apropos of those who had it in mind to get into the field of manufacturing, an interesting survey was sponsored in 1958 by the Canadian National Railways. That survey under the auspices of the railway established a relationship to exist between the growth of a community on the one hand and increased manufacturing employment on the other. According to the survey it was concluded that if simply 100 manufacturing workers are added to a community this is what will occur. There will be a total population increase in that community of 427 persons. One hundred and seventeen more workers will be employed in fields other than manufacturing, for example, construction, utilities, communications. One hundred and thirty-one more households will be created. The school population will increase by 66 pupils. One hundred and eighty seven motor vehicles of all kinds will be registered and 393 new telephones, both business and domestic, will be installed. Three more retail establishments will be constructed and total retail sales in the community will increase annually by almost $1 million. The C.N.R. survey I have just mentioned was based on the addition of 100 workers in the manufacturing field only and is not applicable to additions to any other sectors of employment.
Between 1946 and the end of 1958, if we examine what these immigrants brought with them we find that immigrants brought into Canada approximately $800 million in cash and securities. In addition, they brought with them settlers' effects that had a total value of about $300 million. In the year 1957

alone the newcomers brought to Canada some $101 million in visible assets and $41,800,000 in settlers' effects.
The Minister of Finance must have felt happy if he looked at the books for the year 1957 because he would have ascertained that in that year alone immigrants paid in direct taxation an amount estimated at $190 million, and the accumulated savings of this element of our population in the year 1957 were approximately $146 million.
Statistics are never a very attractive subject matter for a speech. Ordinarily I do not like indulging in reference to them too frequently but you do not get a really accurate picture of the immigrant and his contribution until you study the facts and the figures. I never realized what close track the statisticians keep of all of us until I came across some figures they keep with respect to immigrants in particular.
Using as a base the census figures that were obtained in the year 1951, it has been estimated, it seems with reasonable accuracy, that between 1951 and the end of 1958 immigrants numbered about 1,365,000 and it is believed that in that period immigrants did the following things. They established more than 248,000 households, purchased nearly
173.000	electric or gas ranges, more than
105.000	electric refrigerators, more than
128.000	electric washing machines, more than
72.000	electric vacuum cleaners, more than
207.000	radios and more than 81,000 passenger automobiles. Finally, as I learned from a speech by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) which I read the statisticians have established that these people spoke in a multiplicity of tongues through 120,000 new telephones in their homes.
I have had the advantage of studying pretty carefully many of the excellent
Business of the House
speeches that our Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has delivered during the last few months in various Canadian communities. Many of the statistics to which I have referred derive their authority from her remarks. If she has the opportunity to say so I think she will agree that her speeches disclosing these facts, enlightening as they are, must have startled and amazed the large numbers of fellow Canadians who were included in her audiences. Mr. Speaker, I note that it is six o'clock. May I move the adjournment of the debate?
